prompt: Exercise 1, Part 1: determine the variable generation costs (EUR/MWh_el) of the lignite, the hard coal and the CCGT plant from the data table. Show every conversion step.
solution:
Method: build the cost per MWh_th first, then divide by the electrical efficiency, then add the auxiliary costs.

Step 0 - unit conversion. 1 MWh = 3.6 GJ, so lignite 11.00 GJ/t / 3.6 = 3.06 MWh_th/t, hard coal 25.00 GJ/t / 3.6 = 6.94 MWh_th/t, natural gas 3.33 GJ / 3.6 = 0.9262 MWh_th per unit (the gas 'unit' is 1 MWh_Gas as it is billed, which contains 0.9262 MWh_th).

Lignite: fuel + logistics = 20 + 1 = 21 EUR/t, i.e. 21/3.06 = 6.87 EUR/MWh_th. CO2 cost = 0.40 tCO2/MWh_th x 10 EUR/t = 4.00 EUR/MWh_th. Total fuel-related = 10.87 EUR/MWh_th. Divided by the efficiency of 38 % this gives 28.61 EUR/MWh_el; plus 1.39 auxiliary costs = 30.00 EUR/MWh_el.

Hard coal: the price of 100 USD/t is converted at 1.25 USD/EUR into 80 EUR/t; plus 5 EUR/t logistics = 85 EUR/t, i.e. 85/6.94 = 12.24 EUR/MWh_th. CO2 cost = 0.35 x 10 = 3.50 EUR/MWh_th. Total 15.74 EUR/MWh_th / 40 % = 39.35 EUR/MWh_el; plus 0.65 = 40.00 EUR/MWh_el.

CCGT: fuel + logistics = 25 + 2 = 27 EUR per unit, i.e. 27/0.9262 = 29.15 EUR/MWh_th. CO2 cost = 0.184 x 10 = 1.84 EUR/MWh_th. Total 30.99 EUR/MWh_th / 53 % = 58.47 EUR/MWh_el; plus 1.53 = 60.00 EUR/MWh_el.

Results: 30.00 EUR/MWh_el (lignite), 40.00 EUR/MWh_el (hard coal), 60.00 EUR/MWh_el (CCGT) - exactly the variable costs of PP1, PP2 and PP3 used in Part 2. Two classic traps: the currency conversion USD/EUR, and the fact that the emission factor is given per MWh_th, so the CO2 cost must be added before dividing by the efficiency, never after.

prompt: The hard coal price of 100 USD/t is converted at an exchange rate of 1.25 USD/EUR into ___ EUR/t.
solution: 80 EUR/t. 100 USD/t divided by 1.25 USD/EUR = 80 EUR/t. Together with the 5 EUR/t logistic costs this gives 85 EUR/t, which divided by the heating value of 6.94 MWh_th/t yields 12.24 EUR/MWh_th.

prompt: Which of the following cost items is NOT part of the variable generation costs calculated in Exercise 1, Part 1?
options: The auxiliary costs (e.g. limestone) in EUR/MWh_el
The annuity of the specific investment of the plant
The logistic costs of the fuel (EUR per unit)
The CO2 certificate costs (emission factor times CO2 price)
solution: The annuity of the specific investment is a fixed cost; it belongs to the annualised fixed costs used in the capacity expansion exercise (Exercise 3), not to the variable generation costs. The variable generation costs consist of fuel cost including logistics, CO2 certificate cost, and auxiliary costs - the first two divided by the electrical efficiency because they arise per MWh_th, the auxiliary costs already given per MWh_el.

prompt: Exercise 1, Part 2a: PP1 (240 MW, 30 EUR/MWh_el), PP2 (240 MW, 40 EUR/MWh_el) and PP3 (180 MW, 60 EUR/MWh_el) have to cover a load of 560 MW in hour 8, with no technical constraints. Determine the cost-minimal dispatch, the system marginal costs and the hourly system expenses.
solution:
Apply the merit order: call the cheapest capacity first.

PP1 is cheapest at 30 EUR/MWh and runs at its full 240 MW. PP2 at 40 EUR/MWh runs next and also goes to its full 240 MW. Together they cover 480 MW; the remaining 560 - 480 = 80 MW must come from PP3 at 60 EUR/MWh.

Dispatch: PP1 240 MW, PP2 240 MW, PP3 80 MW.

The system marginal costs are set by the last, most expensive unit that is still free to move - here PP3, which is only partly loaded. Marginal costs = 60 EUR/MWh.

Hourly system expenses = 240 x 30 + 240 x 40 + 80 x 60 = 7,200 + 9,600 + 4,800 = 21,600 EUR.

Note the difference between the two figures the examiner asks for: the average cost of this hour is 21,600/560 = 38.6 EUR/MWh, but the price-relevant number is the marginal cost of 60 EUR/MWh. Inframarginal plants earn the difference as a contribution margin.

prompt: In a cost-minimal dispatch the system marginal costs of an hour are given by the variable costs of the ___ power plant, i.e. the last unit called that is not at its capacity limit.
solution: The marginal (price-setting) plant. It is the last unit called in the merit order that still has free capacity, so an additional MW of load would be produced by it. In hour 8 of the exercise that is PP3 at 60 EUR/MWh; in hour 0 (load 230 MW) it is PP1 at 30 EUR/MWh.

prompt: Exercise 1, Part 2b: minimum stable levels of 60 MW (PP1), 120 MW (PP2) and 120 MW (PP3) are added. Compare hour 7 (load 500 MW) with and without this constraint and explain why the total expenses rise while the marginal costs fall.
solution:
Without constraints (case a) the merit order gives PP1 240 MW, PP2 240 MW, PP3 20 MW. Cost of the hour = 240 x 30 + 240 x 40 + 20 x 60 = 7,200 + 9,600 + 1,200 = 18,000 EUR, and PP3 is the marginal unit, so the marginal costs are 60 EUR/MWh.

With minimum stable levels (case b) PP3 is needed - PP1 and PP2 together give only 480 MW - but it cannot run at 20 MW: its minimum stable level is 120 MW. So PP3 must produce 120 MW, and the cheaper PP2 has to be pushed back to 500 - 240 - 120 = 140 MW. Cost = 240 x 30 + 140 x 40 + 120 x 60 = 7,200 + 5,600 + 7,200 = 20,000 EUR.

The total expenses rise by 2,000 EUR, because 100 MWh are shifted from a 40 EUR/MWh unit to a 60 EUR/MWh unit. At the same time the marginal costs fall from 60 to 40 EUR/MWh: PP3 is now blocked at its minimum and can no longer respond to a small load change, whereas PP2 has free headroom between 140 and 240 MW and therefore becomes the marginal unit.

The lesson: with technical constraints the marginal cost is no longer simply the variable cost of the most expensive running plant - it is the cost of the unit that is actually free to move. Higher system expenses and lower marginal prices can occur simultaneously.

prompt: In part c) of Exercise 1 the plants are additionally limited by their maximum load ramps; PP1 may change its output by at most ___ MW per hour.
solution: 60 MW/h. The maximum load ramps in part c) are 60 MW/h for PP1, 120 MW/h for PP2 and 180 MW/h for PP3. Because PP1 - the cheapest unit - is also the most sluggish, it can no longer follow the steep load rise between hour 5 (200 MW) and hour 6 (380 MW) freely, which is exactly what makes case c) more expensive than case b).

prompt: Exercise 1, Part 3d: read the total system expenses of the three cases off the solution table and explain the pattern. What stays constant?
solution:
The three cases give: a) unconstrained 130,600 EUR, b) with minimum stable levels 135,400 EUR, c) additionally with ramp restrictions 138,600 EUR.

The generated energy is identical in all three cases: 3,820 MWh over the twelve hours (the load has to be covered exactly in every hour, so the total energy cannot change). What changes is only how that energy is split between the units. In a) the split is 2,460 / 1,240 / 120 MWh, in b) 2,460 / 1,000 / 360 MWh, in c) 2,460 / 840 / 520 MWh - energy migrates step by step from the cheap plants to the expensive PP3.

The pattern: every additional constraint narrows the feasible set of the optimisation problem, so the optimal value of the objective function can only get worse or stay the same - the total system expenses rise monotonically, 130,600 < 135,400 < 138,600 EUR. Expressed per MWh the average system cost rises from 34.19 to 35.45 to 36.28 EUR/MWh.

The marginal costs, in contrast, do not move monotonically: in some hours they fall when a constraint is added (hour 7 drops from 60 to 40 EUR/MWh in case b), because the plant that is blocked at a limit is no longer the price-setting unit.

prompt: In case c) of Exercise 1 the solution for hour 6 (load 380 MW) is PP1 = 240 MW, PP2 = 0 MW, PP3 = 140 MW. Why does the expensive PP3 (60 EUR/MWh) run while the cheaper PP2 (40 EUR/MWh) stays off?
solution:
In hour 5 the load is 200 MW and only PP1 runs; PP2 and PP3 are off. In hour 6 the load jumps to 380 MW, i.e. by 180 MW.

PP1 may ramp by 60 MW/h, so it can go from 200 to at most 260 MW, i.e. to its capacity limit of 240 MW. That leaves 140 MW to be covered by a second unit.

PP2 would be the cheaper candidate, but it faces two constraints at once: its ramp rate is 120 MW/h, so starting from zero it can reach at most 120 MW, and its minimum stable level is also 120 MW. It could therefore only deliver exactly 120 MW - which leaves 20 MW for PP3, and 20 MW is below PP3's minimum stable level of 120 MW. That combination is infeasible.

PP3 can do the job alone: its ramp rate of 180 MW/h allows it to go from 0 to 140 MW in one hour, and 140 MW is above its minimum stable level of 120 MW. Cost of the hour = 240 x 30 + 140 x 60 = 7,200 + 8,400 = 15,600 EUR.

The alternative would be to back PP1 down to 140 MW and run PP2 and PP3 at their minima of 120 MW each: 140 x 30 + 120 x 40 + 120 x 60 = 16,200 EUR - 600 EUR more expensive. So the printed solution is the cheaper one. Careful: the Excel solution sheet for part c) prints exactly this second, more expensive variant (139,200 EUR in total instead of the 138,600 EUR on the slide); the slide is the correct optimum.

prompt: In the unconstrained case a) of Exercise 1 the total system expenses over the twelve hours amount to ___ EUR.
solution: 130,600 EUR. It is the sum of 2,460 MWh x 30 + 1,240 MWh x 40 + 120 MWh x 60 = 73,800 + 49,600 + 7,200 EUR. Adding minimum stable levels raises it to 135,400 EUR, adding ramp restrictions on top of that to 138,600 EUR.

prompt: The solution table of Exercise 1 shows the generation of PP1 as 2,460 MWh in all three cases. What does that tell you?
options: PP1 has no technical constraints at all in the exercise
PP1 is the cheapest unit and is never displaced by the minimum stable levels; only the ramp restriction in case c) touches it, and it happens to leave its energy total unchanged
PP1 must be running at its minimum stable level in every hour of the twelve-hour period
PP1 is the marginal plant in every hour, which is why its output is fixed
solution: PP1 is the base-load unit at 30 EUR/MWh; the optimiser always uses it first and it is never pushed back by the minimum stable levels of the other units. Its ramp rate of 60 MW/h is binding only around the steep load rise in hour 6, but the printed solution keeps its energy total at 2,460 MWh. PP1 does have constraints (60 MW minimum, 60 MW/h ramp), it is not always at its minimum, and it is the marginal unit only in the low-load hours 0 to 5.

prompt: Name the most important components of the variable generation costs of a conventional thermal power plant and explain how they are combined into one figure in EUR/MWh_el.
solution:
Four components:

1. Fuel costs - the fuel price per unit (t of coal, MWh of gas) plus the logistic costs per unit, divided by the heating value of the fuel to obtain EUR/MWh_th.
2. CO2 certificate costs - the specific emission factor (tCO2 per MWh_th) times the CO2 price in EUR/tCO2, again in EUR/MWh_th.
3. The electrical efficiency, which converts thermal into electrical energy: the sum of 1 and 2 is divided by the efficiency to give EUR/MWh_el. This is the step where the efficiency does its work - a high-efficiency plant needs less thermal input per MWh_el and is therefore hit less hard by fuel and CO2 prices.
4. Auxiliary costs (e.g. limestone for flue gas desulphurisation, operating materials), which are already given per MWh_el and are simply added at the end.

Formula: c_var = (fuel price + logistics)/heating value + emission factor x CO2 price, all divided by the efficiency, plus auxiliary costs.

What is deliberately not included: capital costs, fixed operating costs and start-up costs. Those are irrelevant for the short-term dispatch decision, which is why the merit order is built on variable costs only.

prompt: Why are power plant outages modelled in energy system analysis at all, and why does the lecture prefer convolution over Monte Carlo simulation?
solution:
Real technical appliances need maintenance and fail from time to time. In the hours in which a plant is off-line it cannot contribute to covering the load, so a model that assumes 100 % availability systematically overestimates the security of supply and underestimates the cost of covering the load.

The exact point in time at which a failure occurs is not known beforehand - but the amount of hours a plant is unavailable is determined by probability and known from historic track records. That is enough to work with: the outage is treated as a probability, not as a scheduled event.

Two methods can be used. Monte Carlo simulation draws a large number of random outage patterns and averages the results; it is easy to implement but the result carries a sampling error and depends on the number of draws. Convolution instead analyses all possible combinations of available and unavailable units analytically, so it provides a more precise result. That is the reason the lecture uses it.

prompt: As an alternative to the convolution method, ___ simulation can be applied to model power plant outages, but it gives a less precise result because it does not analyse all possible combinations.
solution: Monte Carlo simulation. It samples random outage patterns, so its accuracy depends on the number of draws. Convolution enumerates all possible combinations of available and unavailable blocks analytically and therefore provides a more precise result - which is why the lecture chooses it.

prompt: Describe the convolution method 'step by step' as the lecture presents it. Which assumption about outages is made, and what happens to the load in the hours in which a plant is unavailable?
solution:
Step 1: the load duration curve is transformed into a shape with steps of constant load, i.e. it is approximated by a small number of blocks of constant MW over a constant number of hours.

Step 2: the plants are dispatched in merit order, the plant with the lowest cost first.

The basic assumption is that outages may occur at any point in time and are not related to a specific time or season - the outage probability is the same in every hour, independent of the load level. This is what allows the outage to be applied proportionally to every step of the curve.

For the share of hours in which the plant is available, the load is reduced by the plant's capacity. For those hours in which the plant is not available the load is not met - graphically it is not reduced - so other blocks have to cover the load in those time slices. The result is a residual load duration curve with more, smaller steps, which is then handed on to the next plant in the merit order.

Because there is a (very low) probability that all plants fail at the same time, the load can never be met with 100 % certainty, no matter how many blocks are in the system. For modelling purposes the missing energy, which would have to be procured externally, is allocated a very high price - it acts as a backstop technology and its energy volume is the model's measure of unserved demand.
keywords: not related to a specific time

prompt: In the convolution approach the missing energy that would have to be procured externally is allocated a very ___ price, so that the model only uses it as a last resort.
solution: A very high price. The unserved energy is treated as a backstop supply with a prohibitive cost. This has two effects: the optimisation avoids it wherever cheaper capacity exists, and the volume of energy that is nevertheless procured at that price becomes a quantitative measure of the residual supply risk of the system.

prompt: Why can the load never be met with 100 % certainty in a convolution model, no matter how many power plant blocks are in the system?
options: Because the merit order always leaves the most expensive plant out of the dispatch
Because the outage probability of a plant increases with the number of plants in the system
Because the load duration curve is only approximated by steps, which always leaves a rounding error
Because there is a small but non-zero probability that all plants fail at the same time
solution: The outages of the individual blocks are treated as independent events, so the probability that all of them are unavailable simultaneously is the product of their individual outage probabilities - a very small number, but never zero. Hence a residual amount of unserved energy always remains and is priced at a very high value. The stepwise approximation of the load duration curve is a separate modelling simplification and not the reason; the merit order dispatches all plants that are needed; and the outage probability of a single plant is a plant property, independent of how many other plants exist.

prompt: Step 1 of the graphical convolution: describe what is shown in the two diagrams and why the transformation is carried out.
solution:
The left diagram shows a real load duration curve for about 168 hours (one week): the hourly loads sorted in descending order, starting at roughly 8,000 MW, falling steeply in the first 15 hours to about 6,500 MW, then declining almost linearly to about 3,500 MW around hour 160 and dropping to zero at the end.

The right diagram shows the same curve after the transformation into a stepwise constant load: five blocks of constant height, roughly 7,000 MW for the first 30 hours, 5,700 MW for hours 30-60, 5,000 MW for hours 60-90, 4,600 MW for hours 90-120 and 3,500 MW for the remaining hours up to 160.

The purpose: the convolution operates on discrete probability distributions. With a smooth curve every hour would be a separate load level; with a small number of steps each block can be treated as one state with a known duration, and the outage probability of a plant can be applied to that block by splitting it into an available and an unavailable share. The approximation must preserve the energy under the curve (the area) and the peak, otherwise the residual load and the unserved energy come out wrong.

What you lose is chronology: the load duration curve says how many hours a load level occurs, not when - which is precisely the assumption that convolution needs, since outages are also assumed to be independent of the point in time.

prompt: Step 1 of the convolution method transforms the load duration curve into a ___ load, i.e. into a small number of blocks of constant height and known duration.
solution: A stepwise constant load. Each step is a load level of constant height with a known number of hours. This discretisation is what makes the convolution possible: the outage probability of a plant can then be applied to each block by splitting it into an available share and an unavailable share of its hours.

prompt: Step 2 of the graphical convolution: plant 1 has 1,000 MW and an outage probability of 10 %. Explain what happens to the first block of the stepwise load duration curve (7,000 MW for 30 hours) and sketch the result.
solution:
The plant is available in 90 % and unavailable in 10 % of the hours of every block - by assumption the outage is independent of the point in time, so the split applies to each block separately.

For the block of 7,000 MW lasting 30 hours this means:
- in 0.9 x 30 = 27 hours the plant runs at 1,000 MW and the load is reduced to 7,000 - 1,000 = 6,000 MW;
- in 0.1 x 30 = 3 hours the plant is out and the load is not reduced at all, so it stays at 7,000 MW and has to be covered by the following plants in the merit order.

Energy supplied by the plant in this block = 1,000 MW x 27 h = 27,000 MWh. Over the whole 160-hour curve, if the plant is in merit throughout, it supplies 1,000 MW x 160 h x 0.9 = 144,000 MWh.

Graphically: one block of the curve is replaced by two steps - a short high one at the original level (the outage hours) and a long low one at 'level minus capacity'. Doing this for every block and re-sorting the resulting steps in descending order gives the residual load duration curve labelled 'remaining load after dispatch of plant' in the right-hand diagram; the red dotted line is the 'load before dispatch of plant'. The new curve has roughly twice as many steps as the old one - which is why the number of steps has to be kept small at the start.

prompt: Look at the right-hand diagram of the convolution figure: why does the residual load curve still reach the original peak level, and why does it have more steps than the curve before the dispatch?
solution:
The residual curve still touches the original peak because of the outage hours. In the small share of hours in which plant 1 is unavailable (10 % of the hours of the highest block) the load is not reduced at all - the curve keeps the original value of about 7,000 MW. Only in the remaining 90 % of those hours is the load pulled down by the plant's 1,000 MW. Graphically, the residual curve therefore starts with a short spike at the old maximum before dropping to peak-minus-capacity.

That is the whole point of the method: dispatching a plant does not shift the entire load duration curve down by its capacity, it shifts down only the available fraction. Repeating this for every plant means that no matter how much capacity is added, a thin sliver of load at high levels always survives - the load can never be met with 100 % certainty, and the remaining sliver is exactly the expected unserved energy.

The number of steps roughly doubles with every plant, because every existing block is split into an 'available' and an 'unavailable' part, and the resulting pieces then have to be re-sorted in descending order. This combinatorial growth is the practical price of the method's precision and the reason why the initial load duration curve is approximated by only a handful of steps.

prompt: A 1,000 MW plant with an outage probability of 10 % is dispatched against a block of the stepwise load duration curve that is 5,000 MW high and lasts 30 hours. What does the block look like afterwards?
options: 27 hours at 4,000 MW and 3 hours at 5,000 MW
30 hours at 4,000 MW
30 hours at 4,100 MW
3 hours at 4,000 MW and 27 hours at 5,000 MW
solution: The plant is available in 90 % of the hours (27 h), and in those hours the load is reduced by the full 1,000 MW to 4,000 MW. In the remaining 10 % (3 h) the plant is out and the load stays at 5,000 MW. Option A would be the naive result without outages; option B corresponds to reducing the load by the expected capacity of 900 MW in all hours, which is exactly the averaging error that convolution avoids; option D reverses availability and outage.

prompt: The slide asks 'In which way are energy systems likely to develop in future?' and shows a triangle. Name its three corners and explain why they make the future path of the energy system a genuine planning problem.
solution:
The triangle is the classic target triangle of energy policy. Its three corners are economic efficiency, security of supply and environmental compatibility.

The planning problem arises because the three goals are only partly compatible. Pushing environmental compatibility (rapid decarbonisation, phase-out of coal and nuclear) can raise system costs and reduce firm capacity, which touches both of the other corners. Maximising security of supply through large reserve margins or domestic fuels raises costs and may mean burning lignite. Optimising costs alone would keep the cheapest and often the dirtiest assets running. Therefore no unique optimum exists; a weighting between the corners has to be assumed, and different weightings produce different 'optimal' systems.

On top of that the slide places a question mark on the time axis: not only the target state of the future energy system is unknown, but also the path towards it and the time t at which it is reached. This is precisely the reason why the lecture moves on to optimising energy system models (which compute a cost-minimal path once the assumptions are fixed) and to scenario planning (which deals with the fact that those assumptions themselves are uncertain).

prompt: The learning objectives of this section ask you to explain the concept of an 'optimal power plant park' within optimising energy system models. What does 'optimal' mean here, and from whose point of view?
solution:
An optimal power plant park is the combination of installed capacities per technology that minimises the total discounted system expenses of covering the given demand over the whole planning horizon, subject to all technical, resource and policy constraints.

The target function is a cost minimisation for the system as a whole, not a profit maximisation for a single company - that makes it a macroeconomic approach. The model decides on plant commissioning and decommissioning, on the dispatch of the units and on their operation modes; the hard constraint that drives everything is that electricity demand has to be satisfied in every time step.

Two consequences the lecture insists on. First, 'optimal' is only meaningful relative to the input assumptions - demand, fuel and CO2 prices, technology costs, potentials - so the optimal park is the answer to a scenario, not a forecast. Second, the optimal expansion option from a systems perspective need not be profitable from an entrepreneurial perspective: a technology that lowers total system expenses may still fail to recover its own capital costs at the resulting market prices.

prompt: Sketch the input-output structure of an energy systems model as shown on the slide: which groups of inputs enter the market model, and which results does it produce?
solution:
The figure has three columns. On the left the scenario assumptions / energy economic market view, in the middle the market model, on the right the results.

Inputs on the left (scenario assumptions):
- power plant technology development for conventional expansion candidates (capex, opex, efficiency)
- technology development data for renewables (capex, opex)
- regional renewable potentials and generation profiles
- world market fuel price scenarios (hard coal, gas, oil)
- domestic fuel price scenarios (e.g. lignite)
- CO2 certificate limits or prices
- macroeconomic developments (GDP, inflation, exchange rates)
- regional electricity consumption (amount and profile)

Inputs from above: the existing assets and decided projects - the thermal power plant park with installed capacities and efficiencies, and the hydro storages with volumes and discharge rates. From below: external policy-driven developments, e.g. the nuclear phase-out in Germany between 2012 and 2022.

The market model itself minimises the system expenses for load coverage; inside it the figure shows the merit order, i.e. variable costs in EUR/MWh plotted against available capacity in GW, with renewables, nuclear, lignite, hard coal, CCGT and OCGT, against the system (residual) load.

Results on the right: the regional power plant park development, fuel consumption, CO2 emissions, marginal prices (short-run and long-run marginal costs) and the total system expenses.

prompt: Among the results of an energy systems model the slide lists marginal prices, distinguishing short-run marginal costs from ___ marginal costs.
solution: Long-run marginal costs. The short-run marginal costs are the variable generation costs of the marginal unit and set the price when capacity is sufficient. The long-run marginal costs additionally include the annualised investment of the marginal expansion candidate and are the relevant price signal when new capacity has to be built - which is exactly the situation the peak-load pricing theory describes.

prompt: Which model type, target function, variables and constraints does the energy systems model of the lecture use?
solution:
Model type and methodology: a multi-periodic linear programming approach - linear because all cost relationships are formulated as linear functions of the decision variables, multi-periodic because several years or time steps are optimised in one problem.

Target function: minimisation of the decision-relevant expenditures. These comprise, for power plants, the fixed and variable operational costs and the investment, and for the energy flows the fuel costs and the variable transmission costs.

Variables: plant commissioning and decommissioning, unit dispatch, and operation modes.

Constraints: generation capacity, plant availability, fuel resource availability and, if a grid is represented, load flow constraints in the transmission grids.

Driving force: the electricity demand has to be satisfied. That is the hard constraint which forces the model to build and run something in every time step; all other elements only decide what the cheapest way of doing so is. Note the wording 'decision-relevant expenditures' - sunk costs of existing plants do not influence the decision and are therefore excluded.

prompt: Which of the following is a decision variable of the energy systems model described on the slide, rather than an input?
options: The CO2 certificate price
The regional electricity consumption profile
The commissioning and decommissioning of power plants
The world market price of hard coal
solution: Plant (de)commissioning, unit dispatch and operation modes are the model's variables - the model chooses them so as to minimise the decision-relevant expenditures. Fuel prices, CO2 prices and electricity consumption are exogenous scenario assumptions fed into the model from the left-hand side of the input-output diagram; they are the reason why the result is scenario-dependent and not a forecast.

prompt: Fundamental optimisation models distinguish two basic situations. Name them and explain the target function used in each case - and the caveat the lecture adds for the second situation.
solution:
Situation 1 - enough capacity is available. The suppliers make their bids according to their (short-run) marginal costs, and the model's target function is the minimisation of the total system's costs under the hard constraint of load coverage. This is the classical unit commitment / merit order problem: only the dispatch of existing assets is decided.

Situation 2 - new capacity is needed. If demand grows and/or old power plants reach the end of their lifetime, new capacity has to be built. From a systems perspective the 'optimal' capacity expansion option is chosen from a set of alternative options; 'optimal' means the expansion candidate that contributes most to minimising the system expenses. That is a macroeconomic approach: it now includes the investment, so fixed and variable costs have to be traded off against each other - which is precisely what peak-load pricing does.

The caveat: it cannot be concluded that the optimal expansion option from a systems perspective will also be economically profitable from an entrepreneurial perspective. The system optimum minimises total costs, but whether the individual investor recovers his capital depends on the market prices and on the number of hours in which the plant is in the money - a gap that is at the root of the missing-money debate and of capacity mechanisms.

prompt: The lecture warns that the optimal expansion option from a systems perspective need not be economically profitable from an ___ perspective.
solution: Entrepreneurial. The system optimum is defined macroeconomically - the candidate that minimises total system expenses. Whether the individual investor earns his capital back depends on the market prices in the hours in which the plant runs. The two criteria coincide only under idealised conditions (a complete, undistorted market with scarcity pricing); in reality this gap is the origin of the missing-money problem.

prompt: Explain the theory of peak-load pricing using the four diagrams of the slide. How is the cost-minimal technology for a given number of operating hours found, and how are the installed capacities derived?
solution:
Bottom-left diagram - the cost lines. For each technology the annual cost per MW is a straight line in the operating time t: C(t) = C_fix + C_var x t. The intercept is the annualised fixed cost (annuity of the investment plus fixed operating costs), the slope is the variable generation cost. Technologies with a low investment and high variable costs (technology 1) start low and rise steeply; technologies with a high investment and low variable costs (technology 3) start high and rise flatly.

The cost-minimal technology for a given utilisation time is the one on the lower envelope of all these straight lines. The envelope is a convex, piecewise linear curve, and the break points t1, t2, t3 are the utilisation times at which two technologies have equal total costs: t* = (C_fix,B - C_fix,A) / (C_var,A - C_var,B). Technology 4 in the figure never touches the envelope - it is dominated by the others and therefore not built.

Top diagram - the load duration curve. The break points are transferred to the load duration curve: the load level at t1 gives the capacity of the peaking technology, the load at t2 minus the load at t1 the capacity of the mid-merit technology, and so on. The bands P_inst,1 (top, peak), P_inst,2 (middle) and P_inst,3 (bottom, base) are read off in this way, which is why the peak technology is on top of the stack and the base technology at the bottom.

Bottom-right diagram - the price. In each time segment the price equals the variable costs of the technology that is marginal there: C_var1 during the t1 peak hours, C_var2 during t2, C_var3 during t3. The price is therefore highest in the shortest segment - which is exactly what allows the peaking plant, running few hours, to earn its fixed costs.

prompt: In the cost diagram of the peak-load pricing slide, four technologies are drawn but only three appear in the load duration curve. Why is technology 4 not part of the optimal power plant park?
solution:
Because its cost line never lies on the lower envelope. For every utilisation time t between 0 and 8,760 hours there is at least one other technology whose total annual cost C_fix + C_var x t is lower. Technology 4 is therefore dominated: whatever number of operating hours you consider, building technology 4 would raise the total system expenses.

In the figure this is visible from its position: its line runs above technology 2 over the whole relevant range while lying below technology 1 only where technology 2 is already cheaper still. A technology is only built if it wins on some interval of the utilisation time, i.e. if it has both a lower fixed cost than the technology to its left and a lower variable cost than the technology to its right.

This is the general rule for capacity expansion: the optimal park contains exactly those technologies that form the vertices of the lower envelope; any candidate that is dominated in both dimensions - or dominated by a combination of the others - gets zero capacity, no matter how attractive it looks in a single indicator such as the levelised cost of electricity at one assumed utilisation.

prompt: In the peak-load pricing diagram the annual cost of a technology per MW is drawn as the straight line C(t) = C_fix + C_var * t; the cost-minimal technology for a given operating time is found on the ___ of all these lines.
solution: The lower envelope. Since every technology's annual cost is linear in the operating time, the cheapest option for each t is the minimum over all lines; connecting these minima yields a convex, piecewise linear lower envelope. Its break points t1, t2, t3 are the utilisation times at which two technologies are exactly equally expensive, and they are the values that get transferred to the load duration curve to read off the installed capacities.

prompt: Which combination of cost characteristics belongs to the technology that occupies the top band P_inst,1 of the load duration curve, i.e. the peaking technology?
options: Highest fixed costs and lowest variable costs
Lowest fixed costs and lowest variable costs
Highest fixed costs and highest variable costs
Lowest fixed costs and highest variable costs
solution: The peaking technology runs only for the few hours t1 at the top of the load duration curve, so its fixed costs are spread over very little energy. It is only competitive if its investment - and therefore its annualised fixed cost - is as low as possible; it can afford high variable costs because it runs so rarely. Option B describes the base-load technology at the bottom band. Option C would be dominant everywhere and would leave no room for any other technology; option D would be dominated everywhere and never built.

prompt: Exercise 3a: determine the total annualised fixed costs (EUR/MWa) of the four technologies at a WACC of 10 %. Show the annuity calculation.
solution:
The annuity factor for an interest rate i and a lifetime n is a = i(1+i)^n / ((1+i)^n - 1).

For n = 40 years at 10 %: 1.1^40 = 45.259, so a = 0.1 x 45.259 / 44.259 = 0.10226.
For n = 30 years: 1.1^30 = 17.449, a = 0.1 x 17.449 / 16.449 = 0.10608.
For n = 20 years: 1.1^20 = 6.7275, a = 0.1 x 6.7275 / 5.7275 = 0.11746.

Annuity of the investment plus the given fixed operating costs:
- Lignite: 2,200 x 0.10226 = 224.97 EUR/kWa, plus 60 = 284.97 EUR/kWa = 284,971 EUR/MWa
- Hard coal: 1,750 x 0.10226 = 178.95 EUR/kWa, plus 40 = 218.95 EUR/kWa = 218,954 EUR/MWa
- CCGT: 875 x 0.10608 = 92.82 EUR/kWa, plus 25 = 117.82 EUR/kWa = 117,819 EUR/MWa
- OCGT: 450 x 0.11746 = 52.86 EUR/kWa, plus 15 = 67.86 EUR/kWa = 67,857 EUR/MWa

Watch the unit: the question asks for EUR/MWa, so the EUR/kWa figures have to be multiplied by 1,000.

Note on the data: the official Excel solution sheet uses 900 EUR/kW for the CCGT instead of the 875 EUR/kW printed on the slide, giving 95.47 + 25 = 120.47 EUR/kWa = 120,471 EUR/MWa. The graphical solution on the following slides is based on the 900 EUR/kW variant.

prompt: For a lifetime of 40 years and a WACC of 10 % the annuity factor is a = i(1+i)^n/((1+i)^n-1) = ___ (four decimals).
solution: 0.1023 (more precisely 0.10226). With 1.1^40 = 45.259 the factor is 0.1 x 45.259 / 44.259 = 0.10226. Applied to the lignite investment of 2,200 EUR/kW it gives 224.97 EUR/kWa; adding the fixed operating costs of 60 EUR/kWa yields 284.97 EUR/kWa. Note how flat the annuity factor becomes for long lifetimes: for 30 years it is 0.1061 and for 20 years 0.1175, so at a WACC of 10 % a longer lifetime buys surprisingly little.

prompt: Which technology in Exercise 3 has the highest total annualised fixed costs, and roughly how much are they?
options: CCGT, about 118,000 EUR/MWa
Lignite, about 285,000 EUR/MWa
Hard coal, about 219,000 EUR/MWa
OCGT, about 68,000 EUR/MWa
solution: Lignite: 2,200 EUR/kW x 0.10226 = 224.97 EUR/kWa plus 60 EUR/kWa fixed operating cost = 284.97 EUR/kWa, i.e. about 285,000 EUR/MWa. It is the most capital-intensive technology of the set and therefore also the one that needs the largest number of full load hours to pay off - which is exactly why it ends up at the bottom of the load duration curve as the base-load technology. The other three figures are correct for their technologies but are not the highest.

prompt: Exercise 3b: determine the variable generation costs (EUR/MWh_el) of lignite, hard coal, CCGT and OCGT from the table.
solution:
Same scheme as in Exercise 1: cost per MWh_th first, then divide by the efficiency, then add the auxiliary costs of 2.00 EUR/MWh_el.

Lignite (efficiency 44 %): fuel plus logistics = 20 + 1 = 21 EUR/t; divided by 3.06 MWh_th/t = 6.87 EUR/MWh_th. CO2 = 0.40 x 10 = 4.00. Total 10.87 EUR/MWh_th / 0.44 = 24.71, plus 2.00 = 26.71 EUR/MWh_el.

Hard coal (46 %): 100 USD/t / 1.25 = 80 EUR/t, plus 5 = 85 EUR/t; divided by 6.94 MWh_th/t = 12.24 EUR/MWh_th. CO2 = 0.35 x 10 = 3.50. Total 15.74 / 0.46 = 34.22, plus 2.00 = 36.22 EUR/MWh_el.

CCGT (59 %): 25 + 2 = 27 EUR per gas unit; divided by 0.9262 MWh_th = 29.15 EUR/MWh_th. CO2 = 0.184 x 10 = 1.84. Total 30.99 / 0.59 = 52.53, plus 2.00 = 54.53 EUR/MWh_el.

OCGT (40 %): identical fuel, so again 30.99 EUR/MWh_th, but divided by 0.40 = 77.48, plus 2.00 = 79.48 EUR/MWh_el.

Merit order: lignite 26.71 < hard coal 36.22 < CCGT 54.53 < OCGT 79.48 EUR/MWh_el. CCGT and OCGT differ only through the efficiency - the same fuel, the same CO2 factor - which shows very clearly how strongly the efficiency leverages the fuel and carbon price into the electricity cost.

Data note: the official Excel sheet works with an updated gas price of 35 EUR per gas unit instead of the 25 printed on the slide, which raises CCGT to 72.83 and OCGT to 106.47 EUR/MWh_el.

prompt: In Exercise 3 the CCGT and the OCGT burn exactly the same fuel with the same CO2 factor; the only reason their variable costs differ (about 54.5 versus about 79.5 EUR/MWh_el) is their different ___.
solution: The efficiency: 59 % for the CCGT against 40 % for the OCGT. The total fuel-related cost of 30.99 EUR/MWh_th is identical for both; dividing by 0.59 gives 52.53 and by 0.40 gives 77.48 EUR/MWh_el, and adding 2.00 EUR/MWh_el auxiliary costs yields 54.53 and 79.48 EUR/MWh_el. The efficiency acts as a lever on every input that is priced per MWh_th - fuel and CO2 alike.

prompt: Exercise 3c: the system load is equally distributed between 20 GW and 100 GW throughout the year. Determine the installed capacity of each technology in the ideal green-field system. Show the method.
solution:
Step 1 - the total annual cost per MW of each technology as a function of the operating time t: C(t) = C_fix + C_var x t, with the figures from a) and b) (the CCGT taken with 900 EUR/kW as in the official solution):
Lignite 284,971 EUR/MWa + 27 x t; hard coal 218,954 + 36 x t; CCGT 120,471 + 55 x t; OCGT 67,857 + 79 x t (variable costs rounded to whole EUR/MWh as in the solution sheet).

Step 2 - the break-even utilisation times, i.e. the intersections of neighbouring lines, t* = delta C_fix / delta C_var:
Lignite/hard coal: (284,971 - 218,954)/(36 - 27) = 66,017/9 = about 7,335 h
Hard coal/CCGT: (218,954 - 120,471)/(55 - 36) = 98,483/19 = about 5,183 h
CCGT/OCGT: (120,471 - 67,857)/(79 - 55) = 52,615/24 = about 2,192 h
They are strictly decreasing, so all four technologies appear in the optimal park.

Step 3 - transfer the hours to the load duration curve. A uniform distribution between 20 and 100 GW gives the straight line L(t) = 100 - 80 x t/8,760 GW:
L(7,335) = 33.1 GW, L(5,183) = 52.7 GW, L(2,192) = 80.0 GW.

Step 4 - the capacities are the differences between these load levels, read from the bottom of the curve upwards:
Lignite 33.1 GW (base), hard coal 52.7 - 33.1 = 19.6 GW, CCGT 80.0 - 52.7 = 27.3 GW, OCGT 100 - 80.0 = 20.0 GW. Sum 100 GW = the peak load, as it must be on a green field.

This is the pie chart printed on the slide: 33.1 / 19.6 / 27.3 / 20.0 GW. With the higher gas price of the Excel sheet (35 instead of 25 per gas unit) the CCGT is squeezed out almost completely and the mix becomes 33.1 / 42.6 / 9.7 / 14.6 GW - a good illustration of how sensitive a green-field park is to the fuel price assumption.

prompt: Explain how the two diagrams on the right of the Exercise 3 solution slide work together, and why the dashed vertical lines are drawn at the same hour values in both.
solution:
The upper diagram plots, for each of the four technologies, the total annual cost per MW (in million EUR/MWa) against the number of operating hours per year, from 0 to 8,760 h. Each technology is a straight line: intercept = total annualised fixed cost, slope = variable generation cost. OCGT starts lowest and rises steepest, lignite starts highest and rises flattest. Their intersections are the break-even utilisation times, marked by the dashed vertical lines at roughly 2,192, 5,183 and 7,335 hours.

The lower diagram plots the load duration curve of the same year - a straight line falling from 100 GW at hour 0 to 20 GW at hour 8,760, because the load is assumed to be uniformly distributed between those two values.

The dashed lines are drawn at identical hours in both diagrams because the hour axis is the link between the two: a break-even time computed in the cost diagram tells you for how many hours a technology is the cheapest option; reading the load duration curve at that same hour tells you which load level that corresponds to, and hence how much capacity of the technology should be installed. The horizontal dashed lines at 33, 53 and 80 GW are the answers read off in this way.

The direction matters: the technology that is cheapest at long operating times (lignite) is placed at the bottom of the load duration curve as base load; the one that is cheapest at short operating times (OCGT) sits at the top as peak capacity.

prompt: In the green-field optimum of Exercise 3 the peak load is 100 GW and the minimum load is 20 GW. What must the sum of all installed capacities be, and which technology covers the band from 0 to 20 GW?
options: 100 GW in total; the band from 0 to 20 GW is covered by the OCGT
80 GW in total; the band from 0 to 20 GW is covered by the OCGT
120 GW in total, to provide a reserve margin; the band is covered by the CCGT
100 GW in total; the band from 0 to 20 GW is covered by the lignite plants
solution: On a green field without outages, reserve requirements or renewables, the installed capacity must equal the peak load exactly - 100 GW, which is the sum 33.1 + 19.6 + 27.3 + 20.0. The bottom band of the load duration curve is the load that is present in all 8,760 hours; it is covered by the technology with the lowest variable costs and the highest fixed costs, i.e. lignite. The OCGT sits in the top band from 80 to 100 GW and runs only about 2,192 hours a year. No reserve margin is added in this idealised exercise.

prompt: Exercise 3d: what would the average power price be in the ideal supply system? Use the hint on the slide and determine for each technology the number of hours in which it sets the price.
solution:
In each hour the price equals the variable costs of the marginal, i.e. price-setting, technology. The peak technology is marginal in the hours of highest load, the base technology in the hours of lowest load, and the boundaries are exactly the break-even times found in part c).

Hours in which each technology sets the price:
- OCGT: from hour 0 to hour 2,192, i.e. 2,192 h at 79 EUR/MWh
- CCGT: 5,183 - 2,192 = 2,991 h at about 55 EUR/MWh
- Hard coal: 7,335 - 5,183 = 2,152 h at about 36 EUR/MWh
- Lignite: 8,760 - 7,335 = 1,425 h at about 27 EUR/MWh
Sum of hours = 8,760, as required.

Average price = (2,192 x 79 + 2,991 x 55 + 2,152 x 36 + 1,425 x 27) / 8,760
= (173,168 + 164,505 + 77,472 + 38,475) / 8,760 = 453,620 / 8,760 = about 51.8 EUR/MWh.

(With the exact, unrounded variable costs 79.48 / 54.53 / 36.22 / 26.71 the result is 51.75 EUR/MWh; with the updated gas price of the Excel sheet it comes out at 51.91 EUR/MWh - practically the same number, because the higher gas cost is offset by the smaller number of hours in which gas sets the price.)

Interpretation: this is a time-weighted average of the price, not a load-weighted one, and it does not contain any scarcity rent. In this idealised model the peak plant just recovers its fixed costs because the price in the peak hours is its own variable cost only in the marginal hour - in a real market the peaking plant additionally needs scarcity prices above its variable costs to refinance itself.

prompt: In the ideal green-field system of Exercise 3 the technology that sets the price in the roughly 2,200 hours of highest load is the ___.
solution: The OCGT. It occupies the top band of the load duration curve (80 to 100 GW), runs about 2,192 hours a year and has the highest variable costs of the set at 79.48 EUR/MWh; hence it is the marginal, price-setting unit in exactly those hours. In the remaining hours the price falls to the variable cost of the CCGT, then of hard coal, and in the last 1,425 hours to that of lignite.

prompt: The acronym TIMES stands for 'The Integrated ___ EFOM System' and denotes one of the internationally spread optimising energy and material flow models.
solution: MARKAL (Market Allocation Model). TIMES is the successor that merges MARKAL with EFOM-ENV (Energy Flow Optimisation Model - Environment). Further examples on the slide are MESSAGE (Model for Energy Supply System Alternatives and their General Environmental Impact) and the commercial tools Artelys and PLEXOS. The synonyms for this model family are 'energy economic bottom-up models', stressing the technology focus, and 'energy system models', stressing the system aspect.

prompt: The slide lists synonyms for optimising energy and material flow models. Which pair is correct?
options: 'Energy balance models' highlights the technology focus, 'input-output models' highlights the system aspect
'Energy economic bottom-up models' highlights the technology focus, 'energy system models' highlights the system aspect
'Simulation models' highlights the optimisation, 'econometric models' highlights the technology
'Top-down models' highlights the technology focus, 'bottom-up models' highlights the macroeconomic aspect
solution: The lecture gives exactly these two synonyms: energy economic bottom-up models, because the system is built up from individual technologies with their technical and economic parameters, and energy system models, because the whole system is optimised at once. The family is applied not only in the electricity and gas industry but also in process industry, iron and steel, pulp and paper, and in policy analysis; examples are EFOM-ENV, MARKAL, MESSAGE, TIMES, Artelys and PLEXOS.

prompt: Which exogenous data does a capacity expansion model need, and why does the lecture call the provision of these data the major effort of modelling?
solution:
The exogenous data requirements are:
- the power plant park structure and the historical generation mix (generation, demand etc.), used for the calibration of the model on historical data
- energy market developments, above all the price development on the fuel markets
- technical, economic and ecological data of every potentially relevant generation technology for the complete horizon, e.g. 2020 to 2050 - which includes efficiency improvements (for instance for CCGT) and cost degressions, in particular for renewable electricity technologies such as PV and wind
- electricity demand development assumptions
- the market diffusion of new technologies (heat pumps, electric mobility) and its impact on electricity demand

The major effort of modelling is the provision and maintenance of consistent data. Consistency is the key word: the data have to fit each other across technologies, regions and decades. A fuel price path, a CO2 price path and an economic growth path that were taken from three different sources will contradict each other; a cost degression assumed for PV must be compatible with the deployment volume the model itself produces. Because the model results are only as good as this input, an optimisation model is in practice mostly a data project - and this is also the reason why growth curves and experience curves are needed: they are the instruments that generate the technology data for the future in a consistent way.

prompt: Among the exogenous assumptions of a capacity expansion model the lecture explicitly lists cost ___, in particular for renewable electricity technologies such as PV and wind.
solution: Cost degressions. These are the assumed future reductions of the specific investment of a technology, and they are precisely what experience (learning) curves are used to quantify. Together with the assumed efficiency improvements of conventional plants such as CCGT they determine which technology the model chooses in later periods - so a large part of the result is fixed by these input assumptions before the optimisation even starts.

prompt: How is the supply side represented in the model, and which parameter groups does the table on the slide distinguish?
solution:
The European power plant park is aggregated into technology classes - roughly 3 to 4 classes for each energy carrier - categorised according to size, efficiency, investment and so on. Individual units are not modelled; the class is the modelling object. This keeps the linear program solvable while retaining the technological differentiation that the bottom-up approach needs.

The table distinguishes three data groups in the columns - technical data, economic data (split into parameters and conditions/restrictions) and ecological data - and two object levels in the rows:

Installation level: installed capacity, plant availability and technical lifetime as technical data; investment, fixed expenses and economic lifetime as economic parameters; limitations to free de-/commissioning and exogenous expansion as restrictions.

Process level: inputs 1 to 3 and outputs 1 to 3 with their respective share of total input and output, plus the efficiency, as technical data; variable costs, auxiliary fuel costs and ramping costs as economic parameters; limitation of the operating mode to base load, exogenously given operating modes and full load hours as restrictions; emission factors (specific CO2 emissions) and green certificates for renewable electricity generation as ecological data.

The input/output structure with shares is what makes it an energy and material flow model: a class can consume several fuels and produce several products (electricity and heat, for instance) in fixed proportions.

prompt: The table of expansion options gives efficiencies for 2015, 2030 and 2050. What is striking about the way they develop, and how does this connect to the growth curve concept?
solution:
The efficiencies rise between 2015 and 2030 and then stop: CCGT goes from 59.1 % to 62.1 % and stays at 62.1 % in 2050; hard coal (pulverised firing) from 47.2 % to 50.9 % and stays there; lignite from 43.9 % to 49.1 % and stays there; IGCC without CCS reaches 54.0 % in 2030 and remains at 54.0 %. Only the gas turbine still creeps up from 46.0 % to 47.0 %.

This is the assumption of a saturating technical development - exactly the upper plateau of the S-shaped technology growth curve. The technologies are mature: they are approaching the limit of performance set by thermodynamics and materials, so the assumption of further improvement after 2030 would not be defensible. In growth-curve language, conventional thermal plants are basic technologies in the maturity phase, not pacemaker technologies.

The other columns of the table give the specific investment (CCGT 700 EUR/kW, gas turbine 400, hard coal 1,300, IGCC 1,500, lignite 1,500), fixed operating costs (14, 8, 26, 30, 30 EUR/kWa), variable operating costs (0.07 to 0.2 cent/kWh), an amortisation period of 25 years throughout and technical lifetimes of 25 to 40 years. The source is IIP data based on BMU (2010) - which explains why these investment figures are far below the 2024 CAPEX figures on the following slide (CCGT 900 to 1,300 EUR/kW, hard coal 1,700 to 2,300): conventional plant costs have risen rather than fallen since then, which is the opposite of what a naive learning curve would predict.

prompt: The CAPEX table for 2024 gives a low and a high investment figure for every technology. Compare the bandwidths of nuclear, PV utility-scale and CCGT and explain what such a spread means for a capacity expansion model.
solution:
Selected figures from the table (specific CAPEX in EUR/kW, low/high, Fraunhofer ISE and Lazard 2024):
- nuclear 6,000 to 16,000 - a factor of 2.7 between the two ends and by far the most expensive option
- fuel cell 5,000 to 8,000; H2 CCGT 1,100 to 2,400; H2 gas turbine 550 to 1,200
- wind onshore 1,300 to 1,900; wind offshore 2,200 to 3,400; biogas 2,894 to 5,788
- lignite 1,850 to 2,550; hard coal 1,700 to 2,300; CCGT 900 to 1,300; gas turbine 450 to 700
- PV utility-scale 700 to 900 EUR/kWp, PV rooftop small 1,000 to 2,000 EUR/kWp
Battery figures are given per kWh, not per kW: 400 to 1,000 EUR/kWh depending on the segment.

The bandwidths differ strongly. PV utility-scale is narrow (about 30 % spread) because the technology is standardised and built in enormous volumes; nuclear is extremely wide because every project is a one-off with site-specific licensing, financing and construction-time risk. Conventional gas plants sit in between.

For a capacity expansion model this matters twice over. First, the choice within the band decides the result: with 900 EUR/kW the CCGT is a completely different candidate from one at 1,300 EUR/kW - as the Exercise 3 sensitivity shows, a moderate change already reshapes the whole park. Second, a single deterministic value hides the risk: a technology with a wide band should be evaluated in several scenarios rather than with one 'best guess', which is exactly the argument that leads from optimisation to scenario planning.

Note also the unit trap in the table: PV is given in EUR/kWp and battery systems in EUR/kWh, so the figures cannot be compared with the EUR/kW of thermal plants without stating the assumed full load hours or the storage duration.

prompt: According to the 2024 CAPEX table the specific investment of a nuclear plant ranges from 6,000 up to ___ EUR/kW - the widest bandwidth of all technologies listed.
solution: 16,000 EUR/kW. The band of 6,000 to 16,000 EUR/kW reflects the fact that nuclear projects are one-off constructions with site-specific licensing, financing and construction-time risk; recent European projects have overrun their budgets by factors. By comparison, PV utility-scale is quoted at only 700 to 900 EUR/kWp because it is a mass-produced, standardised technology - the practical result of decades of learning effects.

prompt: The slide calls batteries a '(potential?) game changer' and shows the German battery storage build-out from January 2020 to October 2025. Describe what the four diagrams show and why it is relevant for capacity expansion planning.
solution:
The four diagrams (ISEA / RWTH Aachen) show:
1. Installed battery energy capacity in GWh, split into large-scale, industrial and home storage: growth from roughly 1 GWh at the beginning of 2020 to about 23 GWh in October 2025, i.e. more than a twentyfold increase in under six years. Home storage is by far the largest share; large-scale storage only becomes clearly visible from 2023 onwards.
2. The monthly additions in MWh: from a few tens of MWh per month in 2020 to peaks above 600 MWh per month in 2024/25, with large-scale projects appearing as individual spikes.
3. Installed battery power in GW, again split by segment: from below 1 GW to roughly 15 GW.
4. Energy capacity by technology: virtually the entire stock is lithium-ion; lead-acid, NiCd/NiMH, high-temperature and redox-flow batteries are marginal.

Why this matters for expansion planning: peak-load pricing as taught in this chapter assumes that the peak band has to be covered by a peaking generator with low fixed and high variable costs. A battery is a different kind of candidate - it shifts energy in time instead of producing it, so it flattens the residual load duration curve rather than filling its top band. If storage becomes cheap enough, the number of hours in which an OCGT is needed collapses and the whole capacity mix computed in Exercise 3 changes. The energy-to-power ratio (23 GWh over about 15 GW, i.e. roughly 1.5 hours) also shows the current limit: this fleet can cover short peaks, not a Dunkelflaute lasting days.

The question mark in the title is deliberate: the growth is a fact, the system-level consequence is an assumption - and in a model it enters as an exogenous cost degression, i.e. through an experience curve.

prompt: What are growth curves used for in energy systems analysis, and what is the typical shape of the growth rate over time?
solution:
Growth curves support the quantification of technical progress and change. Their goal is to characterise and analyse the growth rates and the limits of technologies - how and when a technology reaches its limit.

The typical pattern: many growth phenomena show growth rates that initially increase over time and then change into decreasing growth rates at a later stage. The cumulated quantity therefore follows an S-shaped curve, while the growth rate itself follows a hump: slow at first because the technology is immature and the market small, fastest in the middle, and falling towards zero as saturation is approached. The lecture illustrates it with a non-technical example, the growth of the body weight of ducks.

Application in energy systems analysis: the examination of the future market penetration of new technologies - the slide names electric mobility - which may have a major impact on the overall development of electricity demand. In other words, growth curves generate the demand-side input assumptions of the expansion model, in the same way that experience curves generate the cost assumptions on the supply side.

prompt: Sketch the basic model of the technology growth curve and name the four phases and the three technology roles marked in the figure.
solution:
The figure plots the technical-functional performance of a technology against time as an S-shaped curve that approaches a horizontal asymptote, the limit of performance of the technology.

Four phases along the time axis:
1. Development - the curve is almost flat, performance improves slowly despite considerable effort.
2. Growth - the steep part, where each unit of effort produces a large gain in performance.
3. Maturity - the curve bends over as the physical or technical limit is approached.
4. Decline - performance stagnates just below the limit; further investment produces almost nothing.

Three roles are attached to the phases: in the development phase the technology is a pacemaker technology (high potential, still unproven, strategically interesting), in the growth phase a key technology (it decides the competitive position), and in the maturity phase a basic technology (everybody has it, it no longer differentiates anyone).

Two further empirical statements accompany the figure: the diffusion of new technologies often lasts many years, and the speed of diffusion differs between industrial sectors, regions or countries, and technologies.

The practical use in modelling: knowing which phase a technology is in tells you whether to assume further improvement (development, growth) or saturation (maturity, decline) - which is exactly the assumption behind the constant post-2030 efficiencies of conventional thermal plants in the expansion data.

prompt: In the technology growth curve a technology in the early development phase is called a ___ technology; in the growth phase it becomes a key technology and in the maturity phase a basic technology.
solution: A pacemaker technology. The sequence pacemaker - key - basic technology maps onto the phases development - growth - maturity of the S-curve. The strategic reading: a pacemaker technology carries high risk but also the largest remaining performance potential, a key technology decides today's competitive position, and a basic technology is available to everyone and therefore no longer a differentiator. In the decline phase the technology stagnates at its limit of performance.

prompt: Summarise the empirical findings on the market penetration of energy technologies (after Lund 2006) that the lecture quotes.
solution:
Four findings:
1. The 'typical' growth rate varies between 4 % and 40 % per year - an order of magnitude of spread, so a single generic diffusion rate cannot be assumed.
2. The time needed to take over 50 % of the estimated market potential, starting from 1 %, varies between 10 and 70 years. Energy technologies diffuse slowly, mainly because the capital stock is long-lived.
3. A saturation close to 100 % is rarely achieved - niches, incumbent technologies and heterogeneous applications remain, so the S-curve usually flattens well below the theoretical potential.
4. The governmental influence is fairly high and the competitive situation is important for the development - diffusion is not purely a technical or cost process; regulation, subsidies and the behaviour of competing technologies shape it.

Consequence for modelling: the diffusion path of a new technology such as electric mobility or heat pumps cannot be derived from the technology alone. It has to be set as a scenario assumption, and the resulting bandwidth of electricity demand is one of the main uncertainties of the whole expansion calculation.

prompt: Empirical analysis of energy technologies shows that the time needed to take over 50 % of the estimated market potential, starting at 1 %, varies between 10 and ___ years.
solution: 70 years. Together with the observed growth rates of 4 % to 40 % per year and the finding that a saturation close to 100 % is rarely achieved, this is the reason why energy system transformations are modelled over decades: the capital stock is long-lived and diffusion is slow, so even a technology that is economically superior today needs a generation to dominate the stock.

prompt: Explain the concept of the experience curve and distinguish it from the learning curve in the strict sense.
solution:
The experience curve is an economic concept that was first discovered in aircraft construction in the early 20th century. Its idea is that the real unit costs decline as the cumulative production volume increases - 'real' because inflation has to be removed, and 'cumulative' because it is the total volume ever produced, not the annual output, that carries the experience.

The distinction: in its original definition the term learning curve refers more narrowly only to the accumulated working time - the labour input per unit falls because workers repeat the same operations. The term experience curve refers more broadly to accumulated production volumes and therefore also captures technical progress, rationalisation, standardisation, the degression of fixed costs and economies of scale.

However, the terms are often used synonymously, and the lecture explicitly states that they will be understood as synonyms in this course. In exam terms: you should be able to name the difference in the original definitions and then say that they are used interchangeably here.

prompt: The experience curve effect was first discovered in the early 20th century in ___ construction.
solution: Aircraft construction. Observations there showed that the labour time - and later the real unit cost - needed for each additional aircraft fell by a roughly constant percentage whenever the cumulative number produced doubled. From this observation the Boston Consulting Group generalised the experience curve as a strategic instrument; today it is one of the standard tools for deriving future technology costs in energy scenarios.

prompt: State the central statement of the experience curve and quantify it. What is plotted against what in the diagram?
solution:
The experience curve describes the functional relationship between the cumulative production volume and the (real) unit cost. The diagram plots the unit costs K/x on the vertical axis against the accumulated production volume x - the 'experience' - on the horizontal axis.

Central statement: if the cumulative production volume increases, the unit costs decrease. The quantification the lecture gives: doubling the cumulative production volume will lead to a unit cost decrease of 20 to 30 %. The figure shows two curves for these two rates; the 30 % curve falls visibly faster and lies below the 20 % curve.

The shape in the linear diagram is a decaying power function: steep at the beginning, then flattening out. This is not saturation in the sense of a physical limit - the relative reduction per doubling stays the same - it is simply the fact that each doubling requires ever more absolute additional volume. Going from 1 to 2 GW installed produces the same percentage cost reduction as going from 100 to 200 GW, but the second step takes a hundred times more deployment.

That is precisely why the curve is redrawn on a double logarithmic scale on a later slide, where the same relationship becomes a straight line.

prompt: According to the experience curve concept as presented in the lecture, what happens when the cumulative production volume of a technology doubles?
options: The real unit costs fall by 20 to 30 % per year
The real unit costs fall by typically 20 to 30 %
The annual production costs fall by typically 20 to 30 %
The real unit costs fall to typically 20 to 30 % of the previous value
solution: The unit costs fall BY 20 to 30 %, i.e. TO 70 to 80 % of the previous value - that residual share is the progress ratio. Option B confuses the reduction with the progress ratio. Option C refers to annual production rather than cumulative volume, which is the decisive quantity: experience is what has been accumulated, not what is produced this year. Option D turns the effect into a time trend, but the experience curve is driven by volume, not by the calendar - a technology that is not deployed does not become cheaper.

prompt: Name and explain the reasons behind the experience curve effect.
solution:
The lecture groups them as follows:

1. Learning effect in the narrow sense: workers become more efficient through the repetition of operations. Handling time per unit falls, error and scrap rates fall.
2. Technical progress: better process technology, better materials, improved product design derived from field experience.
3. Rationalisation: reorganisation of the production process, automation, elimination of unnecessary steps.
4. Standardisation: fewer variants, standardised components and interfaces, which also enables mass production and a supplier industry.
5. Degression of fixed costs and economies of scale: improved workload (utilisation of existing plant), purchasing advantages through larger order volumes, accumulated know-how.

Note that only the first of these is 'learning' in the literal sense - which is exactly why the broader term experience curve is preferred. It also explains why the effect is not automatic: it requires that the additional volume is actually produced and that the organisation exploits it, which is why the precondition on the following slide is that the market can absorb the additional volume or that market share is won from the competition.

prompt: Write down the formal description of the experience curve given on the slide, explain every symbol, and calculate by how much the unit cost falls when the cumulative volume grows from 1 to 1,024 units at a progress ratio of 80 %.
solution:
Formal description: c_i = c_1 * lambda^k, with i = 2^k.

Symbols: c_i is the production cost of the i-th unit, c_1 the production cost of the first unit, lambda the reduction factor with 0 < lambda < 1 (the progress ratio, i.e. the share of the cost that remains after one doubling), and k the number of doublings of the cumulative production volume - defined implicitly by i = 2^k, so k = log2(i) = ln(i)/ln(2).

Calculation: going from 1 to 1,024 units means i = 1,024 = 2^10, so k = 10 doublings. With lambda = 0.80:
c_1024 = c_1 * 0.80^10 = c_1 * 0.1074.
The unit cost falls to about 10.7 % of the cost of the first unit, i.e. by about 89 %.

Cross-check with a rounder case: after 5 doublings (i = 32) the factor is 0.8^5 = 0.328, so about a third of the initial cost. Each doubling always removes the same percentage - 20 % here - which is why the relationship becomes a straight line in a double logarithmic plot.

One remark on the notation: the slide calls lambda the 'reduction exponent', although in the formula lambda is the base and k is the exponent. The quantity that is usually called the progress ratio is lambda; the learning rate is 1 - lambda, here 20 %.

prompt: In the experience curve formula c_i = c_1 * lambda^k the exponent k is linked to the cumulative volume by i = 2^k, so k is simply the number of ___ of the cumulative production volume.
solution: The number of doublings, k = log2(i). This is the whole trick of the formulation: the cost is not a function of time or of the annual output, but of how often the accumulated volume has doubled. Ten doublings correspond to a factor of 1,024 in volume; at a progress ratio of 0.8 they reduce the unit cost to 0.8^10 = 10.7 % of the initial value.

prompt: What are the limitations of the experience curve approach according to the lecture, and where does its strength lie?
solution:
Limitations:
- The approach still lacks a theoretical basis. It cannot explain the specific design of the reduction curves or their slope (Wene 2000); there is no theory that predicts why a technology has a progress ratio of 0.82 rather than 0.75.
- Experience curves are macroscopic models based on the ex-post analysis of empirical data. They describe an aggregate regularity over long periods and large volumes.
- Consequently they cannot form a reliable basis for short-term decisions. Using an experience curve to justify a price for next year's tender is a misuse of the instrument.

Strength: the multitude of empirical observations. The relationship has been found again and again across very different industries and technologies. Typical values of the cost reduction rates lie between 70 and 85 %, i.e. the costs decrease to 70 to 85 % of the initial costs per doubling, although they vary considerably between industries.

A terminological warning for the exam: the slide calls 70 to 85 % a 'cost reduction rate' although it is the share of the cost that remains - the progress ratio. The corresponding learning rate, i.e. the actual reduction, is 15 to 30 %. Note also that the earlier slide quotes 20 to 30 % reduction, i.e. a progress ratio of 70 to 80 %, so the upper end of the two statements does not quite match; the safe answer in the exam is 'roughly 15 to 30 % cost reduction per doubling of the cumulative volume'.

prompt: The lecture states that the typical values lie between 70 and ___ %, i.e. after one doubling of the cumulative volume the costs decrease to that share of the initial costs.
solution: 85 %. The number quoted is the progress ratio - the share of the cost that remains after a doubling - so it corresponds to a learning rate (an actual cost reduction) of 15 to 30 %. Be careful with the wording on the slide, which calls this a 'cost reduction rate'; and note that the earlier slide gives the reduction as 20 to 30 %, i.e. a progress ratio of 70 to 80 %, so the two statements overlap but do not coincide exactly.

prompt: Experience curves are used to support long-term scenarios. What are the main difficulties when they are applied ex ante, i.e. forward in time?
solution:
Experience curves can be an important tool to support the development of long-term scenarios and strategies (IEA 2000) - they are the standard way of generating the future cost assumptions that an energy system model needs. Applied forward in time, however, three difficulties arise:

1. An accurate theoretical prediction of the course of the cost reduction curve is impossible for a new product. Since the approach has no theoretical basis, the progress ratio of a technology that has hardly been built cannot be derived; it can only be transferred by analogy from a comparable technology.
2. Assumptions must be made for the starting point as well as for the level of cost reduction. Both are free parameters, and the result over several doublings depends heavily on them - a progress ratio of 0.80 instead of 0.85 changes the cost after ten doublings by roughly a factor of two.
3. The volume itself is uncertain. The cost falls only if the cumulative volume actually grows, and the volume in turn depends on the cost - a feedback loop that a simple exogenous cost path cannot capture.

Mitigating circumstance the lecture adds: normally there are at least some indications for the expected cost reduction rates, from comparable technologies or from the early data points of the technology itself.

Practical consequence: use a bandwidth rather than a single path, and treat the technology cost assumption as one of the key drivers of a scenario set rather than as a fact.

prompt: Describe the linear representation of the PV module experience curve for 1976-1992. Which values can you read off, and what is the progress ratio?
solution:
The diagram plots the PV module price in US dollars of 1992 per watt peak (US$/Wp) on the vertical axis against the cumulative sales in MW on the horizontal axis, both on linear scales.

Values that can be read off: the 1976 data point lies at a cumulative volume of well under 1 MW and a price of about 48 US$/Wp. The price then falls extremely steeply - by 1 to 2 MW cumulative it is already down to roughly 25 US$/Wp - and the curve flattens out towards the right, reaching about 6 US$/Wp at the 1992 point, where the cumulative sales are roughly 340 MW.

The progress ratio noted in the figure is 82 %, i.e. every doubling of the cumulative sales reduced the module price to 82 % of its previous value - a learning rate of 18 %.

Check of the two end points: from 0.3 MW to 340 MW is a factor of about 1,130, i.e. log2(1,130) = about 10.1 doublings. 0.82^10.1 = 0.13, and 48 x 0.13 = about 6.3 US$/Wp - which is exactly the 1992 value. The relationship is therefore consistent over four orders of magnitude of volume.

The drawback of this linear representation: almost the whole information is compressed into the left-hand edge of the diagram, and the flat right-hand part suggests - wrongly - that the learning has come to an end. That is why the same data are shown again in a double logarithmic plot.

prompt: The same PV data are plotted logarithmically. Why does the experience curve become a straight line in a double logarithmic diagram, and how do you obtain the progress ratio from the slope?
solution:
The experience curve is a power function: c(x) = c_0 * (x/x_0)^b, where x is the cumulative volume. Taking logarithms of both sides gives log c = log c_0 + b * log(x/x_0) - a linear equation in the logarithms. Plotting log c against log x therefore turns the curve into a straight line with slope b, which is why the double logarithmic representation is the standard way of displaying and fitting experience curves.

The link to the progress ratio lambda: one doubling of the volume multiplies the cost by lambda, so lambda = 2^b, i.e. b = log2(lambda) = ln(lambda)/ln(2). For the PV curve with a progress ratio of 82 %: b = ln(0.82)/ln(2) = -0.198/0.693 = -0.286. A decade of volume (factor 10) therefore reduces the price by a factor 10^-0.286 = 0.52, i.e. roughly by half.

What the figure shows: the data points from 1976 at about 0.3 MW cumulative and 48 US$/Wp down to 1992 at about 340 MW and 6 US$/Wp lie almost perfectly on one straight line over three orders of magnitude, with the small staircase symbols marking the successive doublings. The constant slope is the real message: the cost reduction per doubling did not slow down, the doublings simply became harder to achieve.

This representation is also the diagnostic tool: a break in the straight line signals that something structural has changed (a new production technology, a new material, a market distortion), and a fitted straight line is what actually produces the progress ratio used as a modelling assumption.

prompt: The PV experience curve has a progress ratio of 82 %; the corresponding learning rate, i.e. the cost reduction achieved per doubling of the cumulative volume, is ___ %.
solution: 18 %. Learning rate = 1 - progress ratio = 1 - 0.82 = 0.18. Every doubling of the cumulative PV module sales reduced the real module price by 18 %. Over the roughly ten doublings between 1976 (about 0.3 MW cumulative, 48 US$/Wp) and 1992 (about 340 MW, 6 US$/Wp) this compounds to 0.82^10 = 0.14, i.e. a reduction of about 86 %.

prompt: A technology's cost data form a straight line in a double logarithmic diagram of unit cost against cumulative production. What does the straight line tell you?
