options: The technology has reached the limit of its performance and the cost is saturating
The unit cost falls by a constant percentage for every doubling of the cumulative volume
The unit cost falls by a constant percentage per year
The unit cost falls by a constant absolute amount for every additional unit produced
solution: A straight line in a log-log plot means a power law c = c_0 * x^b, which is exactly the statement that a constant relative cost reduction accompanies a constant relative increase in volume - hence a constant percentage per doubling, the progress ratio. Option A would be a straight line in a linear-linear plot; option C would be a straight line in a semi-logarithmic plot against time, and it also mistakes the driver, which is volume, not the calendar; option D would show up as a bend and a horizontal asymptote, which is precisely what the straight line does not show.

prompt: The IRENA figure shows the levelised cost of electricity for CSP, solar PV, onshore and offshore wind from 2010 to 2022. Describe the development and explain how the figure should be read.
solution:
The figure plots the LCOE in 2016 USD/kWh; each circle is an individual project (blue, LCOE database) or an auction result with a single clearing price (orange, auction database), and the thick lines are the global weighted average by year. The shaded horizontal band is the fossil fuel cost range, roughly 0.05 to 0.17 USD/kWh.

Solar PV shows the most dramatic change: the global weighted average LCOE falls from roughly 0.38 USD/kWh in 2010 to below 0.05 USD/kWh around 2020, a reduction of close to 90 %, and the whole cloud of projects moves down with it. Onshore wind falls from about 0.09 to about 0.03 USD/kWh - a smaller relative reduction, because the technology was already mature in 2010. Offshore wind moves from about 0.16 to well below 0.10 USD/kWh, with the auction results (orange) leading the LCOE values by several years. CSP falls from about 0.34 to about 0.08 USD/kWh but remains the most expensive of the four and has by far the fewest projects.

How to read it: by 2020 the averages of PV and onshore wind lie below the lower edge of the fossil fuel band, i.e. the cheapest renewable generation has become cheaper than new fossil generation on an LCOE basis. Note also that the auction values lie below the LCOE values and start earlier - auctions are forward-looking prices for projects to be built, so they anticipate the cost reduction.

The figure is the empirical counterpart of the experience curve: what is drawn here against time is the same effect that the experience curve draws against cumulative volume. A caveat the following slide adds: the LCOE ignores when the electricity is produced, so it does not by itself prove competitiveness.

prompt: The slide is titled 'But ... LCOE might not give you the full picture'. Using the German generation and price chart, explain why a falling LCOE does not by itself decide whether a technology is competitive.
solution:
The chart shows one week of German data (9 to 15 December): the stacked realised generation by technology (PV yellow, onshore and offshore wind blue, lignite, hard coal, gas, hydro, biomass and pumped storage below), the realised consumption / grid load as the red line, and the wholesale prices for Germany/Luxembourg as the dark line against the left axis in EUR/MWh.

What it demonstrates: the price is not constant. In the days with strong wind generation the residual load - load minus renewable feed-in - collapses and with it the wholesale price; in the low-wind period around 12 December the residual load has to be covered by expensive thermal plants and the price spikes to several hundred EUR/MWh.

The consequence for the LCOE: the LCOE is an average cost per MWh over the lifetime and says nothing about when that MWh is produced. But a wind or PV plant produces precisely when all the other plants of the same technology produce, i.e. in hours when the price is low. Its achievable revenue per MWh - the capture price - is therefore systematically below the time-average price, and this gap widens as the share of the technology grows (the cannibalisation effect).

So a comparison of LCOE figures compares costs but not values. A complete assessment has to add the market value of the generation profile, the cost of the flexibility needed to firm it (storage, backup capacity, grid), and the plant's contribution to secure capacity - the very reason why capacity expansion is computed with a system model that minimises total system expenses instead of simply picking the technology with the lowest LCOE.

prompt: How is the demand side represented in a long-term energy system model, and why is the full chronological load curve usually replaced by typical days? Quantify the reduction.
solution:
The model needs the development of the load curves - both the profile and the total demand - for every year of the horizon. A fully chronological consideration of the load, i.e. all 8,760 hours of every model year, can be computationally very expensive, especially in a multi-periodic problem that optimises many years at once.

The common approach is therefore the modelling by typical or representative days. The example on the slide: 8 typical days = 4 seasons x 2 day types. The year is split into spring (92 days), summer (91), autumn (90) and winter (92 days), and each season into working days (about 71 % of the days) and weekend days (about 29 %). Every typical day is then further divided into a few time slices rather than 24 hours - the working day into 0-5, 5-8, 8-11, 11-13, 13-18 and 18-24 h, the weekend day analogously.

Quantitatively: instead of 8,760 hourly time steps per year the model works with 8 typical days x about 6 time slices = roughly 48 load segments, each weighted with the number of hours it represents. That is a reduction of the temporal resolution by more than a factor of 180.

What is gained is tractability, what is lost is chronology: consecutive hours no longer follow one another, so storage cycles longer than a day, ramping constraints and the sequence of scarcity hours can only be represented approximately. This is exactly the trade-off that convolution also makes - it drops the chronology in favour of a duration-based representation.

prompt: A common way of representing the demand side in a long-term model is 8 typical days, obtained as 4 seasons times ___ day types.
solution: 2 - a working day and a weekend day. In the example the working days account for about 71 % and the weekend days for about 29 % of each season, and the seasons comprise 92, 91, 90 and 92 days. Each typical day is additionally split into a handful of time slices, which reduces the year from 8,760 hourly steps to roughly 48 weighted load segments.

prompt: Which target function does a perfect-foresight model use, and why does this approach become computationally expensive?
solution:
In a perfect-foresight model all input assumptions over the whole horizon of calculation are known at the start, and the development of the energy system - in particular the expansion decisions - takes this knowledge into account. The target function is typically the minimisation of the expenses over the complete horizon, formulated as a net present value (NPV) approach: all future expenditures are discounted back to a common reference date and the sum is minimised.

Why it is expensive: because all periods are contained in one single optimisation problem. A decision in 2030 is coupled to the fuel prices and CO2 prices of 2045, so the periods cannot be solved one after another. The number of variables and constraints is roughly the number per period multiplied by the number of periods, and the coupling constraints (the capacity stock carried from period to period) prevent any decomposition. Adding regions, technologies or a finer temporal resolution multiplies the problem again - which is why the temporal resolution is usually reduced to typical days.

The advantage the lecture names is that economically optimal development paths are calculated by the model; the second disadvantage besides the computing effort is that perfect-foresight knowledge is typically not realistic over a period of 30 years - no investor knows the whole path of prices and policies in advance.

prompt: In a perfect-foresight model the target function is typically the minimisation of the expenses over the complete horizon, using an ___ approach so that expenditures of different years become comparable.
solution: An NPV (net present value) approach. All expenditures over the whole calculation horizon are discounted to one reference date and summed, so that an investment made in 2030 and fuel costs incurred in 2045 can be traded off against each other in one objective function. This is precisely what a time-step model cannot do: it only sees the expenses of the individual time step.

prompt: When do a perfect-foresight model and a time-step model produce similar results, and in which situations do they diverge? Give the example the lecture uses.
solution:
For 'smooth' developments of scenarios the two approaches typically achieve similar results concerning the development of the energy system. If demand, fuel prices, CO2 prices and technology costs move gradually and monotonically, then what a step-by-step optimiser decides with limited information happens to coincide with what a foresighted optimiser would have chosen - the near future is a good proxy for the far future.

Differences occur when scenarios include 'shocks'. The example the lecture gives is the sudden start of emission trading in a market where emission trading is not yet implemented. A perfect-foresight model sees the shock coming and prepares for it - it avoids investing in a CO2-intensive plant a few years before the carbon price appears, because the whole lifetime cost is already in its objective function. A time-step model does not see it: it builds the coal plant with the assumptions of the current step, and when the carbon price arrives the plant becomes a stranded asset that is either run uneconomically or written off.

The practical reading: the difference between the two model families is not primarily a question of accuracy but of the question being asked. Perfect foresight answers 'what would an ideal planner do?', the time-step approach answers 'what is likely to happen given how decisions are really made?'. In scenario work with policy discontinuities the divergence between the two is itself an informative result, because it measures the cost of the surprise.

prompt: Which statement correctly describes the time-step approach in energy systems modelling?
options: It is only applicable if the scenario contains shocks such as the sudden start of emission trading
It minimises the discounted expenses over the whole horizon and therefore produces the optimal development path
Only the input assumptions of the individual time step are known to the expansion algorithm; economically optimal development paths cannot be calculated
It is computationally more expensive than perfect foresight because every step has to be solved separately
solution: In the time-step approach the expansion algorithm knows only the assumptions of the individual step, and the target function is the expense minimisation over that step. The advantage is that it is computationally inexpensive and arguably more realistic, since real investment decisions are also taken under limited knowledge; the disadvantage is exactly that economically optimal development paths cannot be calculated. Option A describes perfect foresight; option C reverses the computational effort - solving many small problems is far cheaper than one large coupled one; option D reverses the statement about shocks, which are the case in which the two approaches differ most, not a precondition for using the method.

prompt: The figure distinguishes two decision problems and six sources of uncertainty in competitive electricity markets. Name them and state which uncertainty affects which decision problem.
Which of the listed uncertainties feeds, according to the figure, only into the operational planning / power plant utilisation problem and not into the investment decision?
options: Technological development
Power plant outages
Price uncertainties
The political and regulatory framework
solution: Power plant outages are the only uncertainty in the figure with an arrow leading exclusively to operational planning: a forced outage changes which unit runs this week, but it is a statistical property of the park and does not by itself alter the investment decision. Technological development and the political/regulatory framework point exclusively at strategic planning; load, price and strategic behaviour feed into both.

prompt: What does the lecture mean by 'energy futures', and which three properties does it attribute to them?
solution:
'Energy futures' is the term for long-term scenarios of the energy system. Scenario-based energy systems analyses help to generate cause-and-effect statements about the future development of an energy system - the point is not to predict a number but to make transparent which consequence follows from which assumption.

Three properties:
1. Energy futures are, or ought to be, knowledge-based and systematic. They must rest on documented data and a traceable method, not on wishful thinking.
2. Energy futures are uncertain and are often discussed and perceived controversially - there is no 'right and wrong'. Two well-made scenarios can contradict each other without either being wrong, because they rest on different but equally defensible assumptions.
3. Energy futures are something present. They express present knowledge and present assessments, for instance about relevant technological developments. A scenario says more about what we believe today than about what will happen.

The warning attached: beware of 'manipulated', ideological sketches of the future and of self-fulfilling prophecies. Because there is no right and wrong, a scenario is an easy vehicle for interests - which is why the assumptions, not the results, are what has to be scrutinised.

prompt: In the lecture the term 'energy futures' is used as a synonym for ___.
solution: Long-term scenarios. Energy futures are knowledge-based and systematic, uncertain and controversially discussed (there is no right and wrong), and they are something present - they express today's knowledge and today's assessment of, for instance, technological developments, rather than a prediction of what will happen.

prompt: Summarise in your own words the purpose of scenario planning approaches and the objectives of the different target groups of energy scenarios.
solution:
Purpose. Decision making in the energy sector has a very long time horizon - power plants, grids and storage facilities last for decades - so the relevant uncertainty cannot be removed by better data. Scenario planning is a technique for dealing with this omnipresent uncertainty: instead of one forecast it produces several internally consistent, plausible pictures of the future, so that a strategy can be tested against all of them. Its purpose is to make the key uncertainties explicit, to explore the range of possible developments, and to identify strategies that are robust rather than optimal in one single future.

Target groups. The governmental / political perspective pursues resource security, sustainability and security of supply; its evaluation focus is to find the macroeconomic optimum, i.e. the expense-minimal solution that satisfies all restrictions. The entrepreneurial perspective pursues profit maximisation and risk minimisation; its evaluation focus is to analyse and evaluate the chances and risks associated with investment decisions and to find profitable, robust investment strategies that secure long-term market share.

Why this matters for the scenario construction: the target group determines what a scenario set must be able to do. A public authority needs one consistent expense-minimal path; a company needs a set that allows the same yardstick to be applied to a coal plant, a pumped storage and a wind park, and that allows the isolated effect of single input variations to be evaluated. The same model can serve both, but not the same scenario set.

prompt: The chart shows CO2 certificate prices for 2020, 2030 and 2050 taken from different published scenarios. Read off the spread and explain what such a picture means for an investment decision.
solution:
The chart plots the CO2 price in EUR of 2008 per tonne for a set of published studies (WEO Reference and WEO 450, E[R] Reference, ECF Reference and ECF 80 % RES, EU Trends 2007 and 2009, Eur PowCh) in three time slices.

For 2020 the values range from 17 EUR/t (EU Trends 2009 Reference) to 47 EUR/t (ECF 80 % RES), with most studies between 20 and 34 EUR/t. For 2030 the range widens dramatically: 19 EUR/t at the bottom, 93 EUR/t at the top, a factor of almost five. For 2050 only four studies remain, between 46 and 103 EUR/t.

What it means. The spread is not measurement noise; it is the consequence of different assumptions about climate policy ambition, technology availability and demand. It grows with the time horizon, which is exactly the opposite of what a decision maker would like.

For an investment this is decisive, because the CO2 price is one of the two determinants of the merit order position of a thermal plant. At 20 EUR/t a hard coal plant is well ahead of a CCGT; at around 48 EUR/t - with the cost data of Exercise 1 - the two swap places, and above that gas runs ahead of coal. The entire scenario band therefore straddles the switching point: within the published range, the same coal plant is either a base-load asset or a stranded one.

The correct handling is not to pick the average. It is to evaluate the investment in several scenarios, to identify the switching point explicitly, and to prefer the option that performs acceptably across the band - which is the definition of a robust strategy in scenario planning.

prompt: Define a scenario and explain the sentence 'Scenario planning is NOT forecasting'.
solution:
A scenario describes a possible but by no means certain set of future conditions - for instance the development of prices on the world fuel markets, of electricity demand, of technology costs or of the regulatory framework. It is a consistent combination of assumptions, not a statement about what will happen.

Decision making in the energy sector typically involves a long-term time horizon, which results in high uncertainty, and scenario planning is the technique for dealing with this omnipresent uncertainty confronting decision makers.

'Scenario planning is NOT forecasting': a forecast claims to name the most probable future and is judged by whether it turns out to be right. Scenario planning is rooted in the assertion that all forecasts are wrong. It therefore does not attach probabilities to its futures and does not designate a most likely one; it deliberately spans a range so that a strategy can be tested against several futures at once.

The practical consequence: the quality criterion of a scenario is not accuracy but consistency, transparency and relevance - the assumptions must fit each other, must be documented, and must concern drivers that are both important and uncertain. The figure of the widening cone from today towards 2050 expresses the same idea: the further one looks, the wider the range of futures that must be considered, and narrowing that cone artificially to a single line is the error scenario planning is designed to avoid.
keywords: possible but by no means certain

prompt: Scenario planning is explicitly NOT ___; on the contrary, it is rooted in the assertion that all of these are wrong.
solution: Forecasting. A forecast names the single most probable future and is judged on whether it comes true; scenario planning starts from the assertion that all forecasts are wrong and therefore spans a range of possible but by no means certain sets of future conditions, without assigning probabilities to them. Its quality criterion is consistency and relevance, not accuracy.

prompt: What does scenario analysis do, according to the lecture? Name the four points.
solution:
Scenario analysis does:
1. Acknowledge uncertainty and highlight the key, critical sources of uncertainty and ambiguity. Making the uncertainty explicit - and naming where exactly it sits - is the first product of the exercise, not a side effect.
2. Develop a range of possible future scenarios for exploration, acknowledging that not all are equally likely and that the future may indeed have aspects from more than one scenario. The scenarios are corner points of a space, not mutually exclusive predictions; reality typically lands somewhere between them.
3. Develop a range of strategies and future indicators of which strategies may be most critical. The output is not only pictures of the future but also candidate strategies and the early-warning indicators that tell you which world you are actually drifting into.
4. Acknowledge that future uncertainties may create discontinuities. Trend extrapolation is explicitly abandoned - breaks, shocks and structural changes are legitimate scenario content.

The counterpart, on the following slide, is what scenario analysis does not do: hide uncertainty, develop a single most likely answer, develop a single strategy to commit to, or obtain unavailable data.

prompt: Which of the following is explicitly listed as something scenario analysis does NOT do?
options: Develop a range of future indicators of which strategies may be most critical
Highlight the key, critical sources of uncertainty and ambiguity
Develop a single most likely answer and a single strategy to commit to
Acknowledge that future uncertainties may create discontinuities
solution: Developing a single most likely answer, and a single strategy to which a company can commit, is on the 'does not' list - together with hiding uncertainty or ambiguity and obtaining unavailable data or making decisions on available data that may not be relevant to the future planning process. The other three options are on the 'does' list. The distinction matters in practice: management usually wants exactly the single answer that the method refuses to deliver, and the value of the method lies in resisting that demand.

prompt: Distinguish the top-down and the bottom-up approach to scenario construction and explain what the lecture recommends.
solution:
Top-down ('scenario = consistent story'): one starts from the picture of the future. Pictures of the future and the paths towards those 'target pictures' are defined and described; consistent storylines belonging to those pictures are written; and only then are consistent parameter settings derived that are in line with the storylines. The strength is coherence and communicability - the scenario can be told; the risk is that the numbers are bent to fit the narrative.

Bottom-up ('scenario = combination of parameter settings'): one starts from the parameters. The starting point is the parameter settings and drivers for the different technologies; settings of different parameters are then combined into a scenario, ensuring that no relevant chances or risks for a certain technology are missed. The strength is completeness of the parameter space; the risk is combinations that are individually plausible but jointly incoherent - a high CO2 price together with a high coal capacity, for instance.

The advice of the lecture is to combine the two: build the parameter combinations bottom-up, then assign storylines to those combinations and refine assumptions and descriptions iteratively. The result is called 'narrative scenarios' - quantitatively complete and at the same time tellable, which is what makes them usable both as model input and as a communication instrument.

prompt: If storylines are assigned to parameter combinations and the assumptions are refined iteratively, the lecture calls the result ___ scenarios.
solution: Narrative scenarios. They are the recommended combination of the bottom-up approach (scenario = combination of parameter settings, ensuring that no relevant chance or risk for a technology is missed) and the top-down approach (scenario = consistent story, with target pictures and storylines). The iteration between the two is what makes a scenario both quantitatively complete and communicable.

prompt: The slide warns of a common misunderstanding: top-down versus bottom-up in scenario planning is not the same as top-down versus bottom-up in energy systems modelling. Explain both pairs of terms.
solution:
In scenario planning the pair describes how a scenario is constructed. Top-down means starting from a picture of the future and a consistent storyline and deriving the parameter settings from it; bottom-up means starting from the parameters and drivers of individual technologies and combining them into a scenario. The distinction is about the direction of the construction process - story first or numbers first.

In energy systems modelling the pair describes the resolution and the disciplinary logic of the model. A bottom-up model represents the system through individual technologies with their technical and economic parameters - capacities, efficiencies, investments - and computes the system from these building blocks; the optimising energy and material flow models of this chapter (EFOM, MARKAL, MESSAGE, TIMES) are of this type. A top-down model works with aggregated macroeconomic relationships - elasticities, production functions, sectoral aggregates - and represents the energy sector as part of the whole economy; it captures feedbacks on GDP and employment but has no technological detail.

The two pairs are therefore orthogonal: a bottom-up energy system model can perfectly well be fed with a top-down constructed scenario, and vice versa. Confusing them is a classic exam trap - the words are identical, the meaning is not.

prompt: The selection of a scenario set depends strongly on the targets of the user. Contrast the governmental/political perspective with the entrepreneurial perspective.
solution:
Governmental / political perspective.
Objectives: resource security, sustainability and security of supply.
Evaluation focus of the scenario analysis: find the macroeconomic optimum, i.e. the expense-minimal solution or combination that satisfies all restrictions. This is exactly the target function of the optimising energy system model of this chapter - minimisation of total system expenses under the constraint of load coverage plus the policy restrictions.

Entrepreneurial perspective.
Objectives: profit maximisation and risk minimisation.
Evaluation focus: analyse and evaluate the chances and risks associated with (investment) decisions, and find profitable, robust investment strategies to secure long-term market share.

The difference is not just the objective but the question. The public planner asks 'which system is cheapest for society?' and needs one consistent optimum. The company asks 'which of my options survives in the widest range of futures?' and therefore needs a set of scenarios spanning a band, plus a measure of downside risk. The same model can serve both, but the scenario set cannot - which is why the slide places the choice of the scenario set before the analysis.

The link back to the capacity expansion chapter: this is the same asymmetry as the caveat that the optimal expansion option from a systems perspective need not be profitable from an entrepreneurial perspective.

prompt: A utility wants to use one scenario set to compare an investment in a coal-fired plant, a pumped storage and a wind park. Which evaluation focus does this correspond to?
options: The entrepreneurial perspective, whose focus is to analyse and evaluate the chances and risks of investment decisions
The governmental perspective, because sustainability and resource security determine the value of each option
The governmental perspective, whose focus is to find the expense-minimal solution satisfying all restrictions
Neither, because a single scenario set can never be used for different technologies
solution: This is the entrepreneurial requirement stated on the following slide: a well-balanced evaluation of different strategies, technologies and investment options with ONE scenario set, which is what makes the decisions consistent and comparable. The governmental focus is the macroeconomic optimum, a different question. Option C states the opposite of the lecture's recommendation - using one set is precisely the point, because otherwise the three options would be judged against different assumptions and could not be ranked.

prompt: Why does a scenario set have to be reduced to a manageable size, and which two requirements does a company have concerning such a reduced set?
solution:
In general, many scenarios are imaginable: every driver can take several values, and the number of combinations grows exponentially. In order to avoid an information overflow, a scenario set needs to be reduced to a manageable size. The scenario construction process gives the concrete guidance - reduce the mini-scenarios to a few, 3 to 5, larger scenarios, since experience suggests that managers encounter difficulties coping effectively with much more than three.

The two entrepreneurial requirements concerning the reduced set:
1. A well-balanced evaluation of different strategies, technologies and investment options with one and the same scenario set, allowing for consistency and comparability of different decisions. The example given: it should be possible to achieve a balanced evaluation of the chances and risks of an investment in a coal-fired power plant, a pumped storage and a wind park with the same scenario set. If each option were assessed against its own assumptions, the comparison would be meaningless.
2. The isolated evaluation of the (economic) impact of individual input variations - for example what the impact of a break-through of smart technologies on an investment would be. This is a sensitivity requirement: besides the few full scenarios, one must be able to vary one driver at a time and see what it does.

The two requirements pull in opposite directions - the first wants few, broad, consistent worlds, the second wants many isolated variations - and balancing them is the actual craft of designing a scenario set.

prompt: Name the six steps of a scenario construction process (after Yoe et al. 2004) and say what each of them delivers.
solution:
1. Decide on the key drivers for your scenarios. Determine the most important factors that will decide the nature of the future environment; brainstorm lists of drivers and apply the 80:20 rule so that managers can focus on what is truly important. The decisive selection criterion: look for drivers that are subject to significantly different alternative futures, i.e. factors that are both important AND uncertain. A factor that is important but certain is an assumption, not a driver; a factor that is uncertain but unimportant is noise.
2. Bring the drivers together into a viable framework. Link the critical drivers, construct 'event strings' that connect them so that the linkages and their progression over time become visible, and group the drivers into meaningful combinations.
3. Construct 'mini-scenarios'. Step 2 typically produces 5 to 10 groups of drivers; work out the connections among these groups, decide what each group represents, and develop a mini-scenario around each of them.
4. Reduce the scenarios. Reduce the mini-scenarios to a few - 3 to 5 - larger scenarios, because experience suggests that managers have difficulty coping effectively with much more than three.
5. Write the scenarios. Produce them in the form most suitable for the planners and managers who will use them to develop plans and strategies.
6. Identify issues arising. Examine the scenarios to identify the most critical outcomes and the issues with the greatest impact on the future; the scenarios can then be used in planning.

The logic of the sequence: divergence first (steps 1 to 3, opening the space of possibilities), then convergence (steps 4 to 6, reducing it to something a decision maker can actually work with).

prompt: In step 4 of the scenario construction process the mini-scenarios are reduced to a few, namely ___ larger scenarios, because managers struggle to cope with many more than three.
solution: 3 to 5. Step 2 of the process typically produces 5 to 10 groups of drivers, each of which becomes a mini-scenario in step 3; these are then condensed into 3 to 5 larger scenarios in step 4. The reason given is purely practical - experience suggests that managers encounter difficulties coping effectively with much more than three scenarios - and it is the same argument that lies behind the requirement to avoid an information overflow.
